timeline.title: Born at Jorasanko
timeline.text: Rabindranath was born in the Jorasanko mansion in Calcutta, the youngest of 13 surviving children of Debendranath Tagore and Sarada Devi. His father was a leader of the Brahmo Samaj, a Hindu reform movement. The family called him Rabi.

timeline.title: Travels with his father
timeline.text: After his sacred thread ceremony, the boy toured India with his father for several months. They visited the family retreat at Santiniketan, Amritsar and Dalhousie.

timeline.title: A young writer with a secret name
timeline.text: At sixteen he published his first short story, Bhikharini. He also published poems under the name Bhanusimha, pretending they were lost works of a 17th-century poet. He later called it a joke.

timeline.title: Sent to England
timeline.text: His father wanted him to become a barrister, so he went to a school in Brighton and later briefly read law at University College London. He disliked formal schooling, and it showed in how he later chose to teach.

timeline.title: Home without a degree
timeline.text: In 1880 he returned to Bengal without finishing his studies. He never took a university degree.

timeline.title: His first musical play
timeline.text: He wrote and acted in Valmiki Pratibha, a drama with songs. It was the first of many plays and dance dramas he would write and set to his own music.

timeline.title: Marriage
timeline.text: He married Mrinalini Devi. Wikipedia notes she was about nine at the time; child marriage was common in Bengal then.

timeline.title: Running the family estates
timeline.text: Tagore began managing the family's farm estates at Shelaidaha, now in Bangladesh. The Nobel biography says this work brought him into close touch with ordinary people and grew his interest in social reform. In the same year he published the poetry collection Manasi.

timeline.title: The great story years
timeline.text: From 1891 to 1895, often called his Sadhana period, he wrote more than half of the stories later gathered in Galpaguchchha. They include Kabuliwala (1892). His letters from these years were later published as Glimpses of Bengal.

timeline.title: A school at the abode of peace
timeline.text: At his father's old retreat in Santiniketan, Tagore started an ashram school, later called Patha Bhavana, with only five students. Lessons stressed closeness to nature and few barriers between teacher and pupil, and classes were often held under trees.

timeline.title: Years of loss
timeline.text: His wife Mrinalini Devi died in 1902. Two of his children also died in the years that followed, and his father died in 1905.

timeline.title: A song for a divided Bengal
timeline.text: When the British split Bengal in two in 1905, Tagore wrote songs of protest. Amar Shonar Bangla (My Golden Bengal) is usually dated to this time, though the exact year is disputed because the original manuscript has never been found.

timeline.title: Gitanjali in Bengali
timeline.text: He published Gitanjali, a book of 157 devotional poems in Bengali. Many became songs. The same year saw his novel Gora.

timeline.title: Jana Gana Mana is first sung
timeline.text: A hymn Tagore wrote in December 1911 was sung at the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress. Its first verse would later become India's national anthem. Sources differ slightly on the exact day it was first sung.

timeline.title: Song Offerings in English
timeline.text: Tagore made his own prose translations of his poems, and the India Society in London published them as Gitanjali: Song Offerings, with 103 poems. The poet W. B. Yeats wrote the introduction. Critics later noted the translations were loose, sometimes changing or leaving out parts of the Bengali. The same year he wrote the play Dak Ghar (The Post Office).

timeline.title: The Nobel Prize
timeline.text: Tagore learned he had won the Nobel Prize in Literature, the first given to a non-European. The Swedish Academy praised his verse, which he had made part of the literature of the West "in his own English words". He later gave his prize money to his school and university.

timeline.title: Knighted
timeline.text: The British government made him a knight in the 1915 Birthday Honours.

timeline.title: Lectures in Japan and America
timeline.text: From May 1916 to April 1917 he lectured in Japan and the United States. His essays on nationalism in the West, in Japan and in India were collected in the book Nationalism. In 1916 he also published the novel Ghare Baire (The Home and the World) and the short sayings of Stray Birds.

timeline.title: The world in one nest
timeline.text: Tagore laid the foundation stone of Visva-Bharati, a university meant to bring India and the world together. Its motto means "where the world makes a home in a single nest".

timeline.title: Giving back the knighthood
timeline.text: After British troops killed hundreds of unarmed people at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, Tagore wrote to the Viceroy, Lord Chelmsford, renouncing his knighthood. He wished to stand "shorn of all special distinctions" beside his countrymen.

timeline.title: A school of art
timeline.text: Tagore founded Kala Bhavana, an institute of fine arts, and invited the painter Nandalal Bose to lead it. The exact founding date is not recorded; it celebrated its centenary in 2019.

timeline.title: Visva-Bharati opens
timeline.text: Visva-Bharati was formally founded around 1921. Tagore had raised funds in Europe and the United States from 1919 to 1921, and he had already given his Nobel money to the school.

timeline.title: Helping villages help themselves
timeline.text: In 1921 Tagore bought a manor house at Surul, near Santiniketan. In 1922 he set up the Institute of Rural Reconstruction there, with the Englishman Leonard Elmhirst as director. Its aim was to help villagers solve their own problems rather than have solutions imposed from outside. It grew into Sriniketan.

timeline.title: A visit to South America
timeline.text: Tagore arrived in Buenos Aires in November 1924 and stayed until January 1925. He was one of the most widely travelled writers of his time.

timeline.title: Disagreeing with Gandhi
timeline.text: Tagore and Gandhi respected each other, but they argued openly. In his 1925 essay The Cult of the Charkha, Tagore poked fun at the Swadeshi movement and its focus on the spinning wheel. He was wary of strongly nationalist forms of the freedom movement.

timeline.title: A visit he regretted
timeline.text: On a European tour Tagore met the Italian dictator Mussolini in Rome. He was criticised for it, and later publicly denounced Fascism.

timeline.title: The poet becomes a painter
timeline.text: Tagore had begun drawing and painting at about sixty. In 1930 his pictures were shown in Paris and London and then across Europe. He was probably red-green colour blind, which may explain his unusual colours. In the same year he met and talked with Albert Einstein.

timeline.title: Journey to Persia
timeline.text: In April and May 1932 he visited Iran as a guest of the Shah, and then Iraq. He kept travelling and lecturing into his seventies.

timeline.title: Reason over fear
timeline.text: When Gandhi called a deadly earthquake in Bihar a punishment from God for the sin of untouchability, Tagore publicly criticised him for describing a natural disaster as divine punishment.

timeline.title: Failing health
timeline.text: Late in 1937 he lost consciousness and was close to death for a time. He recovered and kept writing, but a similar illness in late 1940 left him weak for the rest of his life.

timeline.title: The last poem
timeline.text: He dictated his last poem a week before he died.

timeline.title: Death in the house where he was born
timeline.text: Tagore died in an upstairs room of the Jorasanko mansion, the same house where he was born. The next year Visva-Bharati founded Rabindra Bhavana to keep his manuscripts, letters and paintings.

timeline.title: India's national anthem
timeline.text: The Constituent Assembly of India adopted the first verse of Jana Gana Mana as the national anthem.

timeline.title: Bangladesh's national anthem
timeline.text: During its war of independence, Bangladesh's provisional government adopted Amar Shonar Bangla as its anthem; it became official in 1972. Tagore wrote the anthems of two nations, and Sri Lanka's anthem was also inspired by his work.

timeline.title: A World Heritage Site
timeline.text: UNESCO added Santiniketan, the home of Tagore's school and university, to the World Heritage List.

feature.title: School, songs, poems and paintings
feature.lead: Tagore did not stay in one art. He built schools, wrote thousands of songs, told stories, made plays and, late in life, painted. Here are the landmarks of the world he made.

items.label: Patha Bhavana, the school under the trees
items.text: Started with only five students at his father's retreat. Children learned close to nature, often in the open air, with few barriers between teachers and pupils. Later pupils included the economist Amartya Sen.

items.label: Kala Bhavana, the art school
items.text: An institute of fine arts, led by the painter Nandalal Bose at Tagore's invitation.

items.label: Visva-Bharati University
items.text: A university for India and the world, with the motto "where the world makes a home in a single nest". It became a central university of India in 1951.

items.label: Sriniketan, the village institute
items.text: The Institute of Rural Reconstruction studied village problems carefully and helped people solve them themselves, including through crafts and farming.

items.label: Rabindra Sangeet, about 2,230 songs
items.text: Tagore wrote the words and music of more than two thousand songs, on worship, love, homeland and the six seasons of Bengal. He drew on Indian classical music, Bengali folk songs and even Scottish ballads.

items.label: Jana Gana Mana
items.text: A hymn first sung at the 1911 Congress session. Its first verse became India's national anthem in 1950.

items.label: Amar Shonar Bangla
items.text: A song of love for Bengal, usually dated to the protests against its partition. Its tune comes from a song by the Baul singer Gagan Harkara. It became Bangladesh's national anthem.

items.label: Galpaguchchha and Kabuliwala
items.text: Short stories of village and city life in Bengal, many written while he ran the family estates. Kabuliwala (1892) is among the best loved.

items.label: Gitanjali (Bengali)
items.text: 157 devotional poems, many sung as songs. The book behind his Nobel Prize.

items.label: Gitanjali: Song Offerings (English)
items.text: 103 prose poems in Tagore's own English, drawn from Gitanjali and other books. It led to the 1913 Nobel Prize. Free to read today.

items.label: The Post Office (Dak Ghar)
items.text: A short play about Amal, a sick boy who dreams of a letter from the king. It was staged in Dublin in 1913 and, during the Second World War, in the Warsaw Ghetto under Janusz Korczak.

items.label: Stray Birds
items.text: 326 tiny sayings and images, like seeds of poems, published in English in New York.

items.label: Paintings at Rabindra Bhavana
items.text: Tagore began painting at about sixty. Rabindra Bhavana, the Tagore museum at Visva-Bharati, holds 1,580 of his original paintings.

items.label: Paintings at the National Gallery of Modern Art
items.text: India's National Gallery of Modern Art lists 102 works by Tagore in its collection.

items.label: First exhibitions in Europe
items.text: His pictures were first shown in Paris and then London, and toured Europe. In 1937 the Nazi regime removed his paintings from a Berlin gallery.

works.text: His first drama with songs, written at twenty, in which he also acted.

works.title: Manasi
works.text: A collection of poems published the year he began running the family estates.

works.title: Galpaguchchha (stories)
works.text: 84 short stories, more than half written between 1891 and 1895, including Kabuliwala.

works.title: Sonar Tari (The Golden Boat)
works.text: A Bengali poetry collection named among his major volumes.

works.title: The Santiniketan school (Patha Bhavana)
works.text: An experimental school, begun with five students, where learning happened close to nature.

works.title: Amar Shonar Bangla
works.text: A song of love for Bengal, usually dated to 1905 (disputed). Now the national anthem of Bangladesh.

works.title: Gora
works.text: A major novel, published the same year as the Bengali Gitanjali.

works.title: Jana Gana Mana
works.text: A hymn whose first verse became India's national anthem in 1950.

works.title: Gitanjali: Song Offerings
works.text: His own English prose versions of 103 poems, published in London by the India Society.

works.title: Dak Ghar (The Post Office)
works.text: A short play about a sick child longing for the wide world, performed across Europe.

works.title: The Gardener
works.text: Poems in English, translated by the author from the Bengali.

works.title: Ghare Baire (The Home and the World)
works.text: A major novel, translated into English as The Home and the World in 1921.

works.title: Stray Birds
works.text: Short sayings and images, published in English in New York.

works.title: My Reminiscences
works.text: His memories of childhood and youth, in Surendranath Tagore's English translation.

works.title: Visva-Bharati University
works.text: A university meant to join India and the world, funded partly by his Nobel Prize money.

works.title: Institute of Rural Reconstruction (Sriniketan)
works.text: Work to help villagers improve farming, crafts and community life on their own terms.

works.title: Paintings and drawings
works.text: Begun at about sixty; 1,580 original paintings are held at Rabindra Bhavana, Santiniketan.
